profile.name: Tanovar
profile.tagline: The traditional Uzbek tanovar dances standardized by choreographer Mukarram Turgunbaeva.
profile.insight: In 1913, Mukarram Turgunbaeva was born in Shakhrikhan, growing up to create the definitive choreography for the tanovar dances that remains the standard today.
profile.profile: Tanovar refers to the traditional tanovar dances of Uzbekistan, whose standard choreography was produced by Soviet-era dancer and choreographer Mukarram Turgunbaeva. Born in Shakhrikhan in 1913, Turgunbaeva fused traditional Uzbek dance with western classical dance. Her work on these dances continues to be the benchmark by which other performances are judged, celebrated through institutions like the Bahor Ensemble and a dedicated museum in Tashkent.
profile.profile_long: The history and standard execution of the tanovar dances are deeply intertwined with the life and artistic career of Mukarram Turgunbaeva, an influential Uzbekistani choreographer and dancer of the Soviet era. Born on 13 May 1913 in Shakhrikhan within the Andijan Region, Turgunbaeva was orphaned early in life and brought up in the family of an uncle. Her initial introduction to dance came through the agency of her grandmother, setting the foundation for a prolific career that bridged traditional forms and theatrical staging. She later worked as an actress in the experimental theater in Samarkand, expanding her dramatic and performance range. In her performances, Turgunbaeva fused traditional Uzbek dance and western classical dance, presenting versions of each alongside one another to explore new artistic dimensions. Among her most significant contributions are the choreographies she produced for many traditional dances, such as the tanovar dances, which remain the standard by which other performances are judged. Her institutional impact is equally profound; in 1939 she was involved in the establishment of Muqimi, the first musical theater in Uzbekistan, having previously choreographed the ballet Pakhta (Cotton) there in 1933 and worked on Shakhida in 1938. Furthermore, she founded the Bahor Ensemble in 1957, which remains a highly regarded performing group in contemporary Uzbekistan and credits her as the choreographer of many of its repertory pieces. For her extensive artistic output, Turgunbaeva received numerous prestigious accolades, including being named a People's Artist of Uzbekistan, People's Artist of the USSR, multiple Stalin Prizes, the USSR State Prize, the State Hamza Prize, the Order of Lenin, and various orders of the Red Banner of Labor and Badge of Honor. Today, her legacy is preserved not only through her enduring choreography for the tanovar dances and the continuing performances of the Bahor Ensemble, but also through a dedicated museum in Tashkent. This museum houses collections focusing on dance in the 1920s and 1930s, featuring exhibits of costumes, posters, and other memorabilia alongside a collection of recordings of Uzbek folk music.

sections.origins_and_history: Tanovar dances are traditional Uzbek dances whose modern standard was established by Mukarram Turgunbaeva. Born in Shakhrikhan in the Andijan Region in 1913, Turgunbaeva was introduced to dance by her grandmother and later performed in an experimental theater in Samarkand. She fused traditional Uzbek dance and western classical dance, creating choreographies for the tanovar dances that remain the standard by which other performances are judged.
sections.notable_figures: Mukarram Turgunbaeva (1913–1978), an Uzbekistani choreographer, dancer, and People's Artist of the USSR who established the standard choreography for the tanovar dances and founded the Bahor Ensemble.
